analysis.one_liner: Creates an FDA pathway for cheaper copies of biologic drugs, but only after 14 to 16 years of market exclusivity for the originals.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Sen. Judd Gregg with two Republican cosponsors in May 2007, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: For the first time, this bill would let companies win FDA approval to sell biosimilars — near-copies of expensive biologic medicines like Enbrel or Avastin — which could lower prices. But it stacks the deck: no biosimilar could even be approved until 12 years after the original drug, and approval could not take effect until 14 years — 16 if the brand maker adds a new use the FDA deems a significant benefit. It also forbids the FDA from ever designating a biosimilar as interchangeable with the original, requires 'do not substitute' warnings on labels, and bars pharmacies from swapping in a biosimilar unless the prescriber specifically authorized it.
analysis.who_benefits: Brand-name biologic drug makers gain the most: 14 to 16 years of protected market exclusivity on products that in 2007 had no competition at all, plus labeling and dispensing rules that keep biosimilars from being substituted at the pharmacy. Biosimilar manufacturers gain a legal pathway that did not previously exist, and patients taking biologic drugs older than 14 years would eventually see lower-priced copies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Brand-name biologic makers; eventually some patients

how_it_helps.text: Creates the first legal pathway for any company to seek FDA approval of a biosimilar to a licensed biologic product, which did not exist under then-current law.

Lets biosimilar applications for products already approved more than 14 years before enactment take effect soon after enactment — as early as one year — once a product class rule is published, so older biologics could face competition sooner.
Allows a biosimilar approval to become effective even if patent litigation over the product is still pending, rather than waiting for lawsuits to finish.

analysis.who_pays: Patients taking biologic drugs, insurers, and government health programs would keep paying brand-name prices for at least 14 years on each product — longer than the exclusivity period in the law Congress eventually passed in 2010 — and because biosimilars could never be designated interchangeable, savings would come slowly, one prescription at a time.

drawbacks.text: The 14-year floor (16 years for products with a new significant use) is longer than the 12-year period in the Biologics Price Competition and Innovation Act that became law in 2010, delaying price competition for most biologics.

The bill bars the FDA from designating any biosimilar as interchangeable and requires labels warning that the product 'shall not be dispensed in substitution' without prescriber authorization, sharply limiting how quickly biosimilars could win market share and lower costs.

Brand makers can extend protection to 16 years by adding a new use with a 'significant clinical benefit,' and any supplement with new clinical data blocks biosimilars for that use for 3 more years — rewarding minor product tweaks with extra years of monopoly.

Every biosimilar requires a product class-specific rule with a minimum 4-month comment period on a concept paper plus a 6-month comment period on the proposed rule, and the FDA gets up to 2 years to finish — a slow, sequential process before any application can even be submitted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does create a biosimilar pathway where none existed, which is a real consumer good, and its patent provisions let approval proceed despite pending lawsuits. But the 14-to-16-year exclusivity and the ban on interchangeability would have delivered far less savings, far later, than the shorter-exclusivity competing proposals of that era; the design protects incumbent biologic makers first and treats affordability as the leftover.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate sent it to its Health committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Sen. Judd Gregg introduced the bill on May 24, 2007, for himself and Sens. Burr and Coburn, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, markup, or Senate vote — and the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009, so the bill expired.

The United States had no biosimilar approval pathway of any kind for the rest of the 110th Congress; the first one was created in the 2010 health reform law, with a 12-year exclusivity period and an interchangeability route this bill lacked.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name biologic drug makers, which kept 100 percent of their markets without any generic-style competition for the remainder of the decade. Patients continued paying full brand-name prices for biologic medicines with no alternative pathway in law.

sides.party_line_note: Only three Republicans sponsored the bill and no votes were ever taken, so the record shows no partisan pattern of support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill would hand them 14 to 16 years of protected market exclusivity and add labeling and dispensing rules that block pharmacist substitution, locking in their role as sole supplier while patients pay brand prices. Its death preserved the same monopoly in practice, since no biosimilar pathway existed at all.

The bill gives them a legal approval pathway for the first time, and lets approvals take effect despite pending patent suits. But they could never be designated interchangeable and could not be substituted at the pharmacy, so their market would be limited to prescriptions won directly from prescribers.
